articles.title: Initial fuel loading begins at Rajasthan Atomic Power Project’s units 7 and 8
articles.summary: NPCIL begins initial fuel loading at Rajasthan Atomic Power Project units RAPP-7 and RAPP-8 after AERB clearance; RAPP-8 may start commercial operations this year.
articles.body: MUMBAI: Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd (NPCIL) on Saturday commenced initial fuel loading of the 700MWe Rajasthan Atomic Power Stations units RAPP-7 and RAPP-8 at Rawatbhata, marking a significant milestone in India’s nuclear power programme.RAPP-7 and RAPP-7 are indigenous pressurised heavy water reactors.The fuel loading process began after receiving clearance from the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board following rigorous safety evaluations, major system integrity audits and site readiness reviews.With the commencement of the initial fuel loading, unit 8 has entered an important stage of its commissioning journey, stated NPCIL. The next major steps will include what is known as the “first approach to criticality”, marking the start of controlled fission chain reaction, followed by the commencement of power generation.RAPP-8, which is the fourth reactor in the series of sixteen indigenous 700 MWe PHWRs being set up in the country, is expected to commence commercial operation this financial year.NPCIL operates 24 nuclear power reactors totalling to a capacity of 8.78 GWe and has 17 nuclear power reactors, totalling to about 13 GWe, under various stages of implementation.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Jailed former Pak PM Imran Khan undergoes medical check-up amid concerns over health
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan underwent a medical check-up at Adiala Jail amid concerns over his health, according to a media repor.
articles.body: Jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan underwent a medical check-up at Adiala Jail amid concerns over his health, according to a media report on Sunday.Khan, 73, has been in jail since 2023 following his conviction in a corruption case and is currently lodged at the high-security Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.According to Geo News, a specialist team from the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) examined Khan at the jail. The check-up included assessments of his blood pressure, cholesterol levels and eyesight.The medical team was led by a PIMS doctor, with medical staff from the Adiala Jail hospital assisting during the examination, the report said.Khan has previously complained of an eye condition and has been taken to PIMS several times for treatment. His supporters have alleged that his health has deteriorated due to inadequate medical care, a claim that prison authorities have repeatedly rejected.The Supreme Court had ordered on August 18 that Khan be shifted to a private medical facility for treatment. However, he was taken to PIMS, where he underwent medical tests before being returned to jail, news agency ANI cited.His Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party has sought his transfer to Islamabad's Shifa International Hospital for a detailed medical examination and treatment, while raising concerns over his health.The party has also announced a September 27 demonstration seeking Khan's release.Khan has faced multiple legal cases since his removal as prime minister through a no-confidence vote in April 2022, with his health and conditions of detention remaining a recurring issue in Pakistan's political discourse.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: No criminality in death of three sisters who died in sea off Brighton
articles.summary: An investigation by Sussex Police into the deaths off the coast of Brighton has concluded.
articles.body:
A police investigation into the deaths of three sisters in the sea off the coast of Brighton has concluded, with no evidence found of criminality or third-party involvement.

A post-mortem examination found that all three women died by drowning, Sussex Police said.

An inquest will aim to establish the facts of where, when and how the sisters died, the force added.

The police investigation found that the sisters were dropped off by a taxi in Madeira Drive at about 22:20 BST on 12 May.

No evidence was found to suggest that they visited any nightclubs or local businesses in the area at the time, police said.

Up to the point of discovery of their bodies, there was "no evidence the women came to harm by any individuals", the force added.

Ch Supt Adam Hays said: "From the outset of this complex and challenging investigation, we have been acutely aware of the speculation surrounding this incident, the public's unanswered questions and their desire for answers.

"Our priority throughout has been uncovering the truth for the loved ones of Jane, Rebecca and Christina, because at this incident's core there has always been a grieving family coming to terms with an unthinkable tragedy and loss.

"However, our inquiries have now concluded, pending any new information coming to light."

An inquest opened into the deaths in May at Brighton & Hove Coroner's Court and is set to continue early October.

The father of the sisters, who were all living together in Greenford, London, formally identified their bodies.

In a moving tribute, their father previously said that "no words can truly describe the pain of losing three daughters in the prime of their lives".

He described the three as "my joy, my strength, and the beautiful light that filled our family with happiness and love".

articles.title: Indian-origin climber, Nepalese guide killed in Manaslu avalanche
articles.summary: South Asia News: An Indian-origin climber and his Nepalese Sherpa guide were killed in an overnight avalanche at Camp 3 on Mount Manaslu (8,163m) after they continued .
articles.body: An Indian-origin climber and his Nepalese Sherpa guide were killed in an overnight avalanche at Camp 3 on Mount Manaslu (8,163m) after they continued towards the summit while six other climbers turned back amid worsening weather, expedition organisers said on Sunday. Rescuers found Dhrubajyoti Guha and Fursemba Sherpa, both 47, buried inside their tent, taking the autumn season toll on the world’s eighth-highest peak to four.Guha, based near Frankfurt in Germany, graduated in mechanical engineering from Bengal Engineering College, Shibpur (now IIEST Shibpur), in 2002. He had worked with ABB, IBM, Pfizer and Nestlé and was an accomplished ultra-endurance trail runner with 32 UTMB World Series race finishes, including several over 100km. Sherpa was an NMA-registered guide from Nepal’s Makalu region who had summited Everest nine times and also climbed Kangchenjunga, Lhotse, Cho Oyu and Manaslu.Mohan Lamsal, managing director of expedition organiser Makalu Adventure, said conditions deteriorated as the group reached the higher camps. “Six other climbers who decided to retreat from Camp 2 are safe, but Guha and Sherpa decided to make an early summit attempt and headed for Camp III on Saturday evening,” Lamsal told TOI.Contact with the two was lost overnight. “We were alerted around 11.30am on Sunday after they stopped responding. We immediately sent four Sherpa climbers to Camp III to look for them. They dug through the snow and found both inside their tent, buried beneath nearly seven feet of snow,” Lamsal said.Continuing snowfall and avalanche risk prevented the rescuers from bringing the bodies to base camp. “I asked the rescue team to descend to the lower camps because it was not safe to remain there. We will try to bring the bodies down once the weather improves,” Lamsal said.Heavy snowfall began on Friday evening and continued through Sunday, with up to 60cm recorded at base camp, forcing hundreds of climbers to retreat or remain at lower camps. Some teams had begun ascending on Saturday in anticipation of a relatively favourable weather window from Monday, but meteorologists had warned of another spell of bad weather around Wednesday as a system developing over the Bay of Bengal was expected to affect the region.The deaths followed two earlier fatalities on Manaslu this autumn. Singaporean climber Lau Wee Seng, 50, died at around 6,000m while descending from Camp 2 on Sept 17, while Tashi Sherpa, 20, a Nepali high-altitude worker, was found dead inside a tent at base camp on Sept 5.Manaslu has drawn a record 480 foreign climbers this autumn, accompanied by more than 500 Nepali guides and support staff. The latest fatalities took the number of reported mountaineering deaths across the Himalayas and Karakoram this year to at least 24, making 2026 one of the deadliest for climbers in the region in recent years.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Germany’s far-right AfD wins another state election, piling pressure on Chancellor Merz, exit polls show
articles.summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s party is facing a dire set of results in state elections, exit polls show, and is set to be squeezed both by the far-right AfD and parties on the left.
articles.body: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party is facing a dire set of results in state elections, exit polls show, and is set to be squeezed both by the surging far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and parties on the left. The AfD is projected to win the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern on 38%, the exit poll from Germany’s public broadcaster shows, just two weeks after the party had its best result yet in Saxony-Anhalt. Merz’s CDU is currently on 5%, barely enough to seal representation in the largely rural state, piling pressure on his beleaguered leadership. In the other election on Sunday, the left-wing Die Linke party leads in Berlin on 26%, followed by the CDU and the Greens, according to the exit polls. There were audible groans inside the CDU watch party in Berlin as the results were read out for both regions. Merz described the results in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern as a “disaster” in a speech after the exit polls were released. Yet the chancellor remained defiant as he spoke of the need for reform to address Germany’s economic issues and deepening divisions. “The answer cannot be to go back to the good old days,” he said. Prior to Sunday’s projections, the CDU’s worst result in a state election to date was 75 years ago: in 1951, it garnered 9% in Bremen – the only time the party has remained in single digits in a state election. AfD co-leader Alice Weidel was gleeful as the exit polls were announced, telling CNN that her party is “clearly the new people’s party in Germany.” “We have overtaken the CDU, and people want a change of policy,” Weidel said. She described Merz as “strongly damaged,” adding: “I believe the CDU cannot continue with Friedrich Merz, with a weak chancellor.” In Berlin, the AfD is outlooked to come in fourth with 13.5%. While not comparable to its gains elsewhere, the result is a notable sign of how the far right is finding support even in the cosmopolitan capital; in Berlin’s last state parliament election in 2023, the AfD took 9.1% of the vote. Sunday’s elections come at a critical moment for Merz, arriving just two weeks after the AfD delivered a crushing blow to his party with a historic state election victory in Saxony-Anhalt, where it took 44% of the vote. The result sent shockwaves through Germany’s political establishment and intensified speculation over Merz’s future as chancellor. In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, like Saxony-Anhalt a former East German state, the AfD sought to capitalize on anger over Germany’s economic inequalities and dissatisfaction with Merz, while campaigning on a platform of mass deportations of undocumented migrants, an end to military aid in Ukraine and closer ties with Russia. The AfD’s candidate for state premier previously told CNN the party’s approach was comparable to the Trump administration’s “America First” agenda. The election was also a test of popularity for the center-left Social Democratic Party’s Manuela Schwesig, who has governed the state since 2017. Schwesig, the first woman to hold the role of state premier in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, campaigned hard to prevent another AfD breakthrough, warning in her final rally of “dark clouds” in reference to the far-right party. She focused on jobs, education and social cohesion in her campaign. Exit polling put the SPD just behind the AfD, with 36.5% of the vote. The state is facing a severe shortage of skilled workers, thanks to an aging population and lower birth rates. Around 50,000 people from an immigrant background work in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Reuters reported, playing a key part in its economy while running up against far-right anti-immigration sentiment. The political picture in Berlin was markedly different. The capital’s state parliament election was predicted to be a close contest between Die Linke and the CDU. Housing affordability was a central issue during the campaign, after a decade of rising rents in the city and with a major shortage of housing projected in the years ahead.

articles.title: California animal rescue operator charged with felonies for alleged 'inhumane and unsanitary conditions'
articles.summary: Video shows the squalid conditions where 300 animals were found at Christine De Anda's unlicensed Los Angeles County kennel, leading to 35 charges.
articles.body: A California animal rescue operator is facing up to 24 1/2 years in state prison after being charged with 35 felonies and misdemeanors for alleged cruelty to animals, as she is accused of leaving roughly 300 animals living in severe squalor. Christine De Anda, 57, operator of the "Rock ‘N’ Pawz" rescue, faces 12 felony counts of animal cruelty, two felony counts of grand theft of labor, and 21 misdemeanor charges ranging from failure to provide care to operating an unlicensed kennel, according to the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office. Prosecutors requested that her bail be set at $914,500 ahead of her arraignment at the Antelope Valley Courthouse. FLORIDA MAIL CARRIER ACCUSED OF SNATCHING PETS ON ROUTE, TRAPPING 100-PLUS CATS AND DOGS IN ‘HOARDING’ HOUSE "For someone who calls herself an animal rescuer, there’s a fundamental responsibility to protect and care for the animals entrusted to her," Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan J. Hochman said. "Instead, purported rescuer Christine De Anda allegedly left these animals to suffer or die from starvation, dehydration, untreated injuries and painful urine and fecal burns in filthy conditions." "After repeated citations and warnings, Ms. De Anda continued taking in animals she could not care for, leaving hundreds to endure prolonged suffering," Hochman added. "These animal victims cannot speak for themselves and look to us to protect them. My office will hold their victimizer fully accountable for her inhumane actions." The charges stem from a March 20, 2026, search warrant executed by Los Angeles County Animal Care and Control (DACC). Investigators removed more than 300 animals — primarily dogs, but also cats, a pig, a rabbit, a goose and two goats — in what DACC Director Marcia Mayeda called the "largest companion animal search warrant and rescue operation ever conducted" in the department’s history. 117 DEAD DOGS FOUND AT ANIMAL RESCUE, MANY WITH GUNSHOT WOUNDS AS INVESTIGATORS PROBE FOR ANSWERS "More than 300 animals were removed from severely inhumane conditions," Mayeda said. "Animals were living in and saturated with their own excrement, had serious untreated illnesses and injuries, were emaciated, and were forced to live in small crates without adequate room to properly lie comfortably. Our teams have worked tirelessly to stabilize them, provide the medical care they needed, and help them recover." At least one cat was found dead from starvation and dehydration at the start of the investigation, authorities said. FLORIDA MAN ALLEGEDLY KILLS FAMILY'S KITTENS IN FRONT OF TEENAGE DAUGHTER AS FORM OF PUNISHMENT: OFFICIALS "Sadly, despite all efforts, we were unable to save every animal due to the extent of their illnesses and injuries," Mayeda added. "DACC is deeply grateful for the support of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Los Angeles, Pasadena Humane and Kern County Animal Services for assisting us with this rescue and the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office for its commitment to pursuing justice for these animals." The L.A. County DA's Office shared a video on YouTube of the animals at the shelter, showing the conditions that led to the charges. She is accused of violating multiple county codes, including operating an animal kennel without required land-use approval, maintaining unsanitary conditions and having structures with unpermitted construction, plumbing, electrical and grading work.

articles.title: Laura Kuenssberg: I asked Earl Spencer who we should believe, him or the King?
articles.summary: Princess Diana's brother has caused a storm with his new memoir - the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg describes how she put his claims to the test.
articles.body:
When I arrived at Althorp on Thursday to speak to Charles, Earl Spencer, only a handful of people were in evidence in the vast stately home, where Princess Diana had once tapdanced in the hall and rollerskated in the cavernous library.

It was only hours after Buckingham Palace had sent out its blistering statement in response to the explosive claims made in a new book by Earl Spencer. From the particularly English peace of this grand countryside setting, Diana's brother had provoked a storm.

That Palace statement, questioning Earl Spencer's account of the days after his sister's death, was a total contrast to its normal "never explain, never complain" mantra. But it meant that as we sat down, with oil paintings of Earl Spencer's aristocratic ancestors staring down at our TV lights, the interview was not just about his recollections of his sister. It had become about whether the earl, or the King himself, was telling the truth. As we asked Earl Spencer: which Charles are we meant to believe?

That's why it was so important to test Earl Spencer's claims. Was he really sure that the then-Prince Charles had sounded "giddy" after his former wife had died on that terrible night in 1997? Both men, after all, were in a moment of profound shock.

Did the earl, a historian and former journalist himself, have evidence of another of his memories, that Charles had "hissed" at him that the world would "forget her soon enough" ? Why does he, the uncle of William and Harry, think the world needs to hear his version of events from all those years ago?

Earl Spencer was resolute; strong in his conviction that his version of events needed to be told as a matter of record. And he recounted his memories of his conversations with the King in meticulous detail, noting carefully in our discussion that the Palace had not explicitly denied his claims, instead choosing to question his judgement.

Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King

Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana, Earl Spencer tells BBC

There is deep unhappiness and frustration in Buckingham Palace at what Earl Spencer has put into the public domain. Their strongly worded statement tells you everything you need to know about how upset they are. "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss," it said.

Bear in mind that the two Charleses have had a difficult relationship for decades. Even before either of them was born, the Spencers and the Windsors, two aristocratic families, had years of splits and spats. In the past 48 hours, allies on either side have lined up to back the two different accounts, with acolytes of the King suggesting he would never have said such things. Others emerged to back Spencer.

There is no way of being completely sure what exactly happened. There hasn't been an explicit denial, but the Palace has objected in very strong terms to how Earl Spencer has presented the past. But speaking to Diana's brother for about half an hour, I felt he seemed entirely sure in his own mind. His book is carefully constructed to give his account, as well as pay tribute to his sister's life as the 30th anniversary of her death approaches.

After we had spoken, we walked down to the lake on the estate where, on a wooded island, Diana was laid to rest. It's a place where, Earl Spencer told me, she could be safe from intrusion, and is marked as a burial place with a huge stone urn.

We passed the little green rowing boat he uses to go to the island to visit her, and walked to what he calls The Temple. It's an 18th Century building that now bears her name and includes a quote from her and another from his famous eulogy to her. It's a line he now says was specifically intended to be a riposte to the other Charles' suggestion that she would quickly be forgotten: Diana "will never be extinguished from our minds".

Earl Spencer told me he was not being "vengeful" and that he was not trying to damage the monarchy - even saying there was more he knew about the King that he could relate but had chosen not to. But by speaking out so boldly, publishing his book, serialising it in the papers, and speaking to us, the earl was not just paying a moving tribute to his sister, but stirring up the long-running contest for control of Diana's memory.

In the closing moments of our interview, Earl Spencer revealed himself not to be a public figure trying to settle old scores or correct myths about his incredibly famous sister. When I asked how much he missed her, he welled up, and nearly three decades on, the tears still came. He said he missed her every day. "The thing with sibling loss? You never get over it," he said.

Charles Spencer was a young man when his sister died at 36 in the most awful circumstances. He joked about crying as a 62-year-old man at the end of a TV interview in which he'd discussed the monarchy and also made claims about the King that he was well aware would stir up controversy around the world. In the normally hidden world of Althorp, the grief of a brother was still plainly on display – what happened to Princess Diana is not all in the past.

articles.summary: KOCHI: At least six people died after a landslide and flash flood struck Kottakamboor in Vattavada, Idukki, Kerala, on Sunday.Four people from Chokkad.
articles.body: KOCHI: At least six people died after a landslide and flash flood struck Kottakamboor in Vattavada, Idukki, Kerala, on Sunday.Four people from Chokkad were reportedly stranded on rocks and trees near the Anganwadi.Search operations are continuing following reports that more people may be missing in the flash flood. Rescue personnel and local residents are jointly taking part in the search.The flash flood hit Kottappuzha at TK Colony in Pookkottumpadam around 5 pm on Sunday. According to preliminary information, around seven people, including tourists and a local woman, were feared to have been swept away.Earlier, the body of a man aged around 50 was recovered from the river at Muttikkund in Pottikkallu. His body was shifted to the District Hospital, while a search was underway for others feared missing.A large number of tourists were present at various locations along the river, from Olarvattom Canal to T.K. Colony, which are popular tourist spots. As it was a holiday, hundreds of people had gathered at Kettungal, Aanakkundu, Balawadippadi and other areas along the Koyipra foothills.After the water level suddenly rose, around 27 people who were stranded in the middle of the river were rescued by local residents and members of the Muhammad Suhail Treatment Aid Committee.However, several people remained stranded at different locations for a long time as they were unable to reach safety.Police, Fire and Rescue Services personnel, volunteers and residents continued rescue operations for those stranded in the river.A search operation was also underway for those feared to have been swept away in the flash flood.Meanwhile, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued a rainfall alert, with seven districts, including Thiruvananthapuram and Idukki, under a yellow alert for Sunday.Isolated heavy rainfall of up to 115.5 mm is expected over a 24-hour period. articles.title: Photos: Nepal flood survivors find little trace of former lives
articles.summary: Nepal’s floods displace thousands, with survivors mourning loved ones and searching for belongings amid the debris.
articles.body:
When Anusa Thapa Magar rushed home from her job in the Maldives after hearing of Nepal’s devastating floods, she clung to the hope that her grandmother had somehow survived.

Instead, when she reached Betrawati, the small riverside town where her family lived, she found only a flat expanse of hardened grey silt.

“If my house is buried underneath, that means my Aama is still here underneath too, right?” the 23-year-old said quietly, standing where the family’s two-storey home once stood. Her grandmother, who could barely walk, was last seen resting on her bed.

Last month’s torrent of mud, rock and water, triggered by a glacial collapse in the mountains along the Nepal-China border, tore through settlements along the Trishuli River, killing at least 1,386 people on the Nepal side. Authorities say 5,130 are still missing, and while searches continue, it has been days since anyone was found alive.

To reach what used to be Betrawati, survivors now climb a steep hillside, cross a narrow ridge and descend into a wasteland. Along the route lie scattered shoes, school ties and children’s backpacks – “silent evidence”, residents say, of the panic as people scrambled to flee the surging floodwaters.

Garment business owner Kalpana Thapa Magar, 43, recalled the moment a friend phoned from upstream. “Run! Run!” she was told. “I just ran. When I looked back, everything was gone, even the people who had been running behind me,” she said.

Downstream in Devighat, shattered shells of houses still stand. Some residents pick through the rubble for belongings, but many say there is no reason to return; the land itself has vanished beneath debris.

For many here, the disaster reopens wounds from Nepal’s 2015 earthquake, which killed nearly 9,000 people. Teacher Sita Thapa Magar, 45, Kalpana’s older sister, said that after the quake, families were at least able to rebuild on their plots. “This time, we have lost everything,” she said. “Our houses, our land, our future.”

On a single broken floor tile – the last visible trace of her home – 61-year-old Shanti Dangol clutched a photograph of the three-storey lodge she once ran for pilgrims and trekkers.

“Economically, people here had started doing well,” she said. “Now, nothing remains.”

articles.title: A Wyoming-to-Canada wildlife project has supported 204 crossings and helped protect 59 million acres; 33 years after it began, it is a finalist for Prince William's Earthshot Prize
articles.summary: US News: A conservation project connecting wild habitats from Wyoming to Canada’s Yukon has been named a finalist for Prince William’s Earthshot Prize. The Yel.
articles.body: A conservation project connecting wild habitats from Wyoming to Canada’s Yukon has been named a finalist for Prince William’s Earthshot Prize. The Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative has spent 33 years protecting 59 million acres of land and supporting 204 wildlife crossings across North America. The non-profit project is one of 15 global finalists for the 2026 environmental award, according to The Associated Press. The project brings together scientists, private landowners, local governments, and Indigenous communities across the Rocky Mountains. By building wildlife overpasses, underpasses, and safety fences along major highways, the initiative helps large animals move safely through their natural habitats without being hit by vehicles.Tracking wildlife across bordersThe idea for the cross-border wildlife corridor began in the early 1990s after researchers tracked a radio-collared wolf named Pluie. Satellite data showed that the wolf travelled across three US states and two Canadian provinces. Her movements showed scientists that individual parks and nature reserves were not large enough to support animals such as wolves, grizzly bears, and caribou over the long term. These findings led to the official creation of the Yellowstone to Yukon initiative in 1993. Its goal was to connect broken-up habitats across a 2,100-mile mountain range.Highway crossings reduce animal deathsBusy highways are one of the biggest dangers for wildlife moving through the Rocky Mountains. To reduce deadly crashes, the organization has worked with transport authorities to build special wildlife crossings. In places such as Banff National Park in Alberta, overpasses and underpasses covered with native plants have reduced collisions between vehicles and hoofed animals by 96 per cent. The organization has also worked to reconnect isolated grizzly bear populations. According to project records, the distance between separated bear groups in the United States has been reduced from 240 kilometres to 75 kilometres.Indigenous leadership strengthens conservationIndigenous communities manage or share management of about one-quarter of the protected land within the corridor. These partnerships have helped several threatened species recover from very low numbers. In northern British Columbia, an Indigenous-led project to protect the Klinse-Za caribou herd helped its population increase from 38 animals in 2013 to 187. Dr Jodi Hilty, President and Chief Scientist of the initiative, said successful conservation requires long-term cooperation between communities. "Being selected as an Earthshot Prize Finalist gives this extraordinary region a chance to be recognised around the world," Hilty said in a press release. "Yellowstone to Yukon is not only a story about wilderness; it is a story about the people who live here and the choices they are making to protect a shared home."Global recognition for conservationFounded by Prince William in 2020, the Earthshot Prize gives five annual £1 million awards to projects working to repair environmental damage. The Yellowstone to Yukon initiative is a finalist in the Protect and Restore Nature category. Prince William praised the 2026 finalists before the official awards ceremony, which is scheduled to take place in Mumbai in November. "Every year, our finalists give me renewed optimism," Prince William said in an official statement. "They show us that, even as the environmental challenges remain urgent, extraordinary people around the world are already proving that progress is possible. Seeing solutions work gives us all confidence to act." The initiative plans to protect another 50 million acres and help create at least 50 more wildlife crossings by 2030.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Central Colombia forest fire threatens tourist town of Villa de Leyva
articles.summary: The country has battled multiple wildfires amid record-breaking temperatures fuelled by El Nino and drought conditions.
articles.body:
A massive wildfire has broken out in central Colombia, threatening the popular tourist town of Villa de Leyva, according to local officials.

The forest fire is near the Andean town in the Boyaca department, with flames engulfing the San Marcos hillside above the colonial architecture and cobblestone streets that attract more than a million visitors annually.

The blaze has already consumed 40 hectares of native forest, sending massive plumes of smoke that are visible from the town’s central square, according to Colombian authorities.

On Saturday night, Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella posted on X that “Villa de Leyva is not alone”, pledging to mobilise all state resources to fight the fire and protect “this historical jewel” and “beautiful city that is the pride of Colombia”.

To combat the flames, the Boyaca department government said it is dispatching two aircraft. A military helicopter will also join the effort, along with firefighters from the capital, Bogota, Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara said.

The mayor of Bogota, Carlos Fernando Galan, will be sending a team of firefighters to join local crews from Tunja and Boyaca, reinforcing containment efforts and securing the urban centre, Lara said.

In the equatorial Andes, forest fires peak during the dry season, but this year they are fuelled by a severe El Nino weather pattern. Record high temperatures and lack of moisture have turned vast expanses of the Andean vegetation into tinderboxes. That has intensified a crisis that has already started 18 active wildfires across the country, according to the latest official data from Colombia’s National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD).

The impacts of El Nino, a natural weather pattern, are felt globally and do not affect the entire South American continent in the same way, inducing extreme droughts in some regions and torrential flooding in others. This year, it comes supercharged by the effects of climate change, which is worrying many scientists, governments and aid workers.

The warming of the adjacent Pacific has triggered catastrophic flash floods and landslides in countries such as Peru and Ecuador.

Unlike in the southern part of the continent, where countries including Argentina, Chile and Uruguay have been expecting unseasonably heavy rainfall, El Nino has the opposite effect in the northern part of the continent. A significant reduction in rainfall leads to severe drought conditions which can suppress cloud formation and displace normal rain patterns, driving average temperatures well above normal.

The soaring heat rapidly evaporates moisture from the ground and water basins, leaving countries such as Colombia with extended periods of drought and critically low precipitation.

“El Nino can bring devastating climate extremes on its own, but it’s unfolding today on a much warmer planet, increasing the likelihood that heat, drought, floods and fires will push communities and ecosystems beyond anything they have experienced before,” said Stephanie Roe, lead climate scientist with the World Wildlife Fund.

articles.title: German state elections: Chancellor Friedrich Merz vows to stay on despite 'disaster' in polls
articles.summary: Exit polls show damaging losses for Merz's centre-right CDU party in the states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
articles.body:
Embattled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay on despite exit polls in two local elections suggesting damaging defeats for his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party.

In the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the party was projected to only just scrape into parliament, while the far-right AfD was on track to win the most votes. Merz called the result "a disaster" for his party.

In Berlin, the ruling CDU was also expected to be beaten by Die Linke (The Left).

Merz is under mounting pressure, with poor approval ratings and rumours he could even be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap.

Votes took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved as the Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Echoing comments he made after that defeat, Merz told reporters at the party's Berlin headquarters on Sunday that he would forge ahead with his coalition government's plans to push through a package of economic, tax and welfare reforms.

"The reforms have to come," he insisted. "I am taking on this responsibility, because I want to move our country forward".

"What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness and patience," Merz said. "I will demonstrate this as CDU party chairman and, above all, as chancellor of our country."

"I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the authoritarian poison that, with the fascination of authoritarianism, is penetrating ever deeper into our society," Merz added.

As the projected results came up on the screen at the CDU's election night gathering in Berlin, there were no cheers or celebration.

This is a party that knows it's in trouble, and its leader quickly went on the offensive, declaring that he is going nowhere.

Merz has long coveted the top job in German politics, and likely won't give it up easily.

Polls for both states closed at 18:00 local time (17:00 BST), with a final result expected later on Sunday night, or even Monday morning.

Public broadcasters ZDF and ARD put the AfD ahead in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. The party was projected to take 38% of the vote share in the state, according to ZDF, followed in second place by the centre-left SPD, on 36%. The CDU was on 5% of the vote.

However, the AfD is unlikely to govern in the state as other parties refuse to work with it.

For Berlin, the broadcaster put the CDU on 20% of the vote share when polls closed, behind Die Linke on nearly 26%.

Prior to Sunday's elections, there had been intense speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced unless his party's political fortunes improved.

Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz, who has only been chancellor for 16 months.

On Sunday, Burkard Dregger, a CDU member of the Senate in Berlin, told the BBC it was right that Merz should stay on. "He has a lot of work to do and we don't have time to waste to form new government in the federal level".

He described the electorate as "impatient", adding that it was "not realistic to expect that every issue has been solved within one year.

"He has got four years and we have to give him the four years," Dregger said.

While his backers have argued that many of the problems the nation faces are inherited, Merz himself is deeply unpopular.

The former corporate lawyer's tack to the right on issues like immigration has failed to erode AfD support, while also alienating people further to the left.

articles.title: Kelsey Parker welcomes baby after 'devastating' stillbirth
articles.summary: The widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker has given birth after last year announcing the "devastating" loss of a stillborn baby.
articles.body:
Kelsey Parker, the widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker, has welcomed a baby after last year announcing a "devastating" stillbirth.

The podcaster and author, 35, had two children with British boy band star Tom Parker before he died in 2022 , aged 33, after being diagnosed with terminal brain cancer.

She is now in a relationship with Will Lindsay and last June revealed the "earth-shattering news" that they had lost their baby Phoenix.

On Sunday, a post on her Instagram account showed a photo of a newborn baby's arm next to a pink sign with the word River. "Welcome to the world, River. Our little bit of hope," the caption said.

Celebrities including The Saturdays singer Rochelle Humes, TV presenter Susanna Reid and reality TV star Holly Hagan-Blyth have congratulated Kelsey Parker on social media.

"Congratulations angel," Rochelle Humes wrote.

"Oh my goodness – this is so wonderful – welcome River," Susanna Reid said.

Hagan-Blyth commented "I am SO happy for you xxxx".

Kelsey Parker's Instagram bio says "turning life's hardest moments into hope".

Last year she posted a poem online after the loss of her stillborn baby.

It was called Born Sleeping, Forever Loved, and began "the world grew quiet as you arrived, So loved, so longed for, yet not alive. Our precious boy, our angel light, Born with wings, took silent flight".

In 2023, she published a book titled With And Without You, about the first year after the death of her former partner Tom.

The couple married in 2018 and had a daughter, Aurelia Rose, and a son, Bodhi.

In a post after his death she wrote "thank you to everyone who has supported in his care throughout, he fought until the very end. I'm forever proud of you".

Her latest pregnancy was announced in May in an Instagram post that said "somehow, through all the heartbreak, it feels like Tom and Phoenix have sent us another little gift from heaven, our little rainbow baby".

articles.title: ‘When do I blow entire nation up?' Trump's ultimatum after Iran warns of 'decisive war'
articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trump warned on Sunday that he has arrived at a critical turning point in the conflict with Iran, stating that serious consequence.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump warned on Sunday that he has arrived at a critical turning point in the conflict with Iran, stating that serious consequences would follow if Tehran does not change course.Speaking in an interview with Fox News about his approach to the ongoing war, Trump said, "My question is, if and when do I blow the entire nation up? They had better behave".Laying out the options before him, the US President said he could destroy the country, allow it to collapse economically, or seek a diplomatic resolution, while predicting that "very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future".Trump's remark arrives amid reports that the US and its regional allies were preparing to resume operation against Iran.Responding to the reports, Iran's central command stated that any US attack would be met with retaliation "without any limitations or considerations".Iranian Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the country needed to pursue both military action and negotiation at the appropriate moment."We believe that the duality of war or negotiation is not real, but that we must both fight and negotiate. We must fight sensibly and decisively and negotiate with authority and rationality at the right time," Ghalibaf told the Iranian Parliament.He described Iran's diplomatic stance as "completely clear, rational, and non-negotiable," and said Tehran's conditions had already been passed on to the other side via mediators."The enemy knows very well that the path of deception and unilateral imposition is closed," Ghalibaf said.On Saturday, Iran relayed its seven conditions for a truce to the US through Qatari mediators, warning that it would close the Strait of Hormuz and pursue a "decisive war" if Washington rejects its demands.Al Jazeera reported that Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's supreme national security council, said Tehran was awaiting a response from Trump.Ahead of the UN general assembly's high-level week beginning Monday, Trump signaled openness to diplomacy, saying he would "probably be open" to talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: See inside the abandoned 95-year-old LA church that just became a luxury hotel
articles.summary: Hotel Lucile transformed a 1931 Silver Lake church in Los Angeles into a 25-room boutique hotel, preserving stained glass and wood flooring.
articles.body: A building that has stood in Los Angeles for nearly a century is welcoming visitors in an entirely new way after an extensive restoration. The former Bethany Presbyterian Church, built in 1931 in the city's Silver Lake neighborhood, has been converted into Hotel Lucile, a 25-room boutique hotel with a courtyard cocktail pool that opened Sept. 14, according to a hotel news release shared with Fox News Digital. The property has taken on several roles over the decades. After operating as a church, it was later used as a theater and an antique market before being converted into a hotel, according to the release. RENTALS NOW ALLOWED IN HISTORIC WATER TOWER ON KING CHARLES' SANDRINGHAM ESTATE WHERE ROYALS SPEND CHRISTMAS The latest transformation was about seven and a half years in the making, Anthony Gutierrez, opening general manager of Hotel Lucile, told Fox News Digital. The restoration focused on finding a new use for the building while maintaining elements that date to its time as a house of worship, Gutierrez said. Many of the church's original features remain throughout the property, including stained-glass windows, wooden beams, high ceilings and steel-framed windows. One of the biggest transformations took place inside the former chapel, which now serves as the hotel's restaurant and dining room. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "Literally just about every aspect of the chapel itself was preserved," Gutierrez said, pointing to the original wood flooring, beams and stained-glass windows. Preserving those features while preparing the building for its new use required extensive work, Gutierrez said. Crews removed the chapel's original wood flooring to install modern electrical and plumbing systems and add soundproofing for the guest rooms before putting the flooring back into place. "For the dining room itself, it is as original as it can be," he said, estimating that about 90% of the space remains original. Working with a building approaching 100 years old also presented challenges throughout the years-long redevelopment. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "We had surprises up until the day when we received our certificate of occupancy," Gutierrez said. "It was not an easy journey." Meeting modern requirements while trying to preserve the building's original architectural elements made parts of the restoration a "painstaking" process, he added. The building's latest chapter also includes an art collection, with two large hand-painted murals in the former chapel and other works displayed throughout the property. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Some pieces are part of a permanent collection, while others are available for purchase, Gutierrez said. Along with preserving elements of the former church, the property has introduced modern touches, including an Erewhon-curated minibar and a roving martini cart that makes its rounds each evening, according to the release. Gutierrez said the combination of old and new can offer travelers something different from a traditional hotel experience. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "There is some comfort in things being the same, but taking even a small risk of just going somewhere different and experiencing something different can really bring kind of a highlight to a trip or even a staycation," he said.

articles.title: ‘Disastrous’: Germany’s Merz faces mounting pressure after fresh CDU defeats
articles.summary: Europe News: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz suffered a fresh electoral setback on Sunday as his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) lost ground in two state electio.
articles.body: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz suffered a fresh electoral setback on Sunday as his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) lost ground in two state elections, but he rejected suggestions that his government would backtrack on its reform agenda.Exit polls by public broadcaster ARD showed the CDU securing just 5% in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, its lowest-ever result in a German state since World War II.In Berlin, the centre-right party was projected to finish second with 20%, trailing the Left party, which was estimated to win 24.5%, according to ARD's exit poll.Merz described the CDU’s performance as a “disaster” but remained defiant, arguing that Germany’s economic and political challenges made difficult, and potentially unpopular, reforms more necessary rather than less. He pledged to continue his agenda with “backbone, steadfastness and patience.”His authority had already been weakened by the CDU’s defeat to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the September 6 election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. The result had shocked many Germans, triggering protests in several cities in Europe's biggest economy.Since becoming Germany’s leader in May 2025, Merz has pledged to revive an economy that has seen little growth for years. But he has struggled to improve the country’s gloomy national mood and has himself become increasingly unpopular.Merz losing ground?Meanwhile, the anti-immigration and Russia-friendly AfD made significant gains on Sunday as well.The AfD’s strong performance in Saxony-Anhalt, where it has its strongest opportunity yet to lead a far-right state government since World War II, has further weakened Merz’s position nationally. In recent weeks, calls for his replacement as chancellor have even emerged from within his own party, although no prominent allies have publicly backed his departure, and many have cautioned against getting drawn into “personnel debates.”Apparently bracing for a difficult period following the elections, Merz cancelled a planned trip to New York next week to attend the UN General Assembly. articles.title: Burnham hails Greenland deal ahead of first Trump meeting in US
articles.summary: While Burnham praised the agreement, Lib Dem leader Ed Davey called it a "pretend" victory for Trump.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has hailed a deal between Denmark and the US to "strengthen security in the Arctic" after the two countries resolved a months-long feud over Greenland.

The UK prime minister and his Danish counterpart Mette Frederiksen "welcomed the US's commitment to the region" in a call on Sunday morning, Downing Street said.

Nato previously said the agreement would help stabilise the region, as Trump declared Denmark would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs" in the semi-autonomous Danish territory in the Arctic.

Burnham's comments come as he is expected to meet Trump for the first time at the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in New York this week.

Nato welcomes Greenland deal as Trump says it will give US 'permanent security control'

The agreement comes after months of threats by Trump to "take" Greenland over national security concerns, citing its strategic location for defence purposes as well as its mineral wealth.

No text of the agreement has been released, but Trump said in a Truth Social post the deal came with "no cost to the United States" and meant it could "do what is necessary" to "secure and defend the security of Greenland".

He said it included a rule that no US adversary could maintain a military presence in Greenland or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval".

In a readout of Sunday's phone call, a No 10 spokesperson said Burnham and Frederiksen "welcomed the US's commitment to the region and underlined the strategic and shared importance of the High North for Euro-Atlantic security".

The spokesperson added: "The Prime Minister congratulated Prime Minister Frederiksen and the Kingdom of Denmark on negotiating a deal benefiting the US, Greenland and Denmark, and said he would pass on his congratulations to President Trump."

While Burnham praised the agreement, Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey called it a "pretend" victory and a near carbon copy of the existing agreement.

"Donald Trump is trying to claim he's got a success in Greenland, but actually, all he's got is almost a carbon copy of the agreement that's persisted since the 1950s," he said at a Q&A with members at party conference.

"So let Donald Trump try to pretend he's had a victory. The truth is, Europe, Nato, countries like Canada stood up to him and won."

Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China.

In the wake of the deal, Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week.

The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.

The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted.

Burnham has spoken with Trump at least twice since entering Downing Street and No 10 said he intends to use the UNGA to "drive forward work on issues that matter to people at home" including the cost of living and the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Meloni promises to ban burqas, niqabs in Italy’s schools
articles.summary: Prime minister of Italy’s longest serving government since WW2 faces election threat from far-right rival party.
articles.body:
Italy will ban burqas and niqabs in schools, as well as limit the number of foreign students in classes, said far-right Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, with immigration expected to be a central issue in next year’s general election.

Meloni outlined the proposed changes on Sunday at a gathering of the youth wing of her nationalist conservative Brothers of Italy (FdI) party, adding that they would also make Italian language lessons compulsory for parents of foreign students having “serious difficulties integrating into the school system”.

“For us, anyone who comes to Italy and wants to build their future here must learn our language, understand our culture, and respect our rules,” she said to a standing ovation at the Gioventu Nazionale national festival in Rome. “It is the only serious way to welcome them.”

Once approved by the government, the changes would need parliamentary approval within 60 days to pass into law.

Meloni’s right-wing administration is Italy’s longest-running government since the end of the Second World War , but her party is expected to face a serious challenge in 2027 from the National Future (FN) party, which is further to the right of the FdI and its popularity has been rapidly increasing in polls since February.

FN called for a crackdown on the wearing of burqas in schools in July.

Burqas are full-face veils sometimes worn by Muslim women that hide the entire face, including the eyes. Niqabs are similar, but the eyes are visible.

Neither covering is expressly banned in Italy, but a 1975 law prohibits the use of helmets or garments that make identification difficult without a justified reason.

A 2008 ruling later clarified that full-face coverings may be worn for religious or cultural reasons if the face is revealed when identity verification is required.

However, the anti-immigrant League party, which is part of Meloni’s ruling coalition, submitted a bill earlier this year that would ban helmets or garments, except in specific circumstances such as sporting events or places of worship.

Alongside the burqa ban, Meloni said she would implement a legal cap on the number of foreign students per class.

However, a 30 percent limit on foreign students per class and school already exists under Italian law and Meloni did not spell out how that would change.

Foreign students currently make up about 12 percent of enrolment in Italian schools.

articles.title: Trump tariffs hit Canada’s dairy farmers as US sales stall
articles.summary: A 50 percent tariff has disrupted dairy exports, leaving Canadian farmers with milk that cannot be redirected overnight.
articles.body:
Abbotsford, British Columbia – Every second day, 28,000 litres of raw milk leave Casey Pruim’s farm in Abbotsford in western Canada, entering a distribution system built on the assumption that the milk and the products made from it will have somewhere to go.

While most is consumed in Canada, some had been sold across the border to the United States.

Those sales have largely come to a standstill since US President Donald Trump’s 50 percent tariff on $20bn in Canadian goods, including dairy products, came into effect on August 22.

Pruim, who is also chair of the British Columbia Dairy Association representing about 400 dairy farmers across the province, told Al Jazeera that Canadian farmers do not individually decide which products are exported.

Instead, producers such as Pruim – whose farm has 330 cows milked three times a day – sell into the provincial milk-marketing system, which distributes milk to processors according to demand, including for products exported to the US.

If a processor loses US demand, it may require less milk, with the impact then spread across the provincial pool.

Dylan Kruger, director of public affairs at BC Dairy, told Al Jazeera “there is still considerable uncertainty around the impact of the US tariffs”.

He said it was too early to know how the industry would be impacted or whether milk no longer sold to the US could be sold elsewhere, mitigating financial losses.

But the tariffs and wider trade tensions have already introduced uncertainty and instability for businesses.

“If the processor who’s exporting some of his product to the United States can no longer sell into that market because he’s now priced out of the market with a 50 percent tariff, that’s how it would impact the dairy farm,” Pruim said.

Pruim said if processor demand is squeezed, farmers would be forced to dump the milk. In the worst-case scenario, the herd has to be cut.

“Cows aren’t like a tap; you can’t just turn them on or off,” he said.

His warning captures dairy’s particular vulnerability in a tariff war: Milk is highly perishable, collected on a tight schedule and dependent on processors whose demand can change much faster than farmers can adjust production.

“These tariffs are completely unwarranted,” David Wiens, president of the Dairy Farmers of Canada, told Canada’s CBC News, adding that they would affect “the supply chain, not only in Canada but in the US as well”.

Dairy trade between Canada and the US has largely operated under a free trade agreement between the US, Mexico and Canada, known as CUSMA in Canada.

Canada manages the supply of dairy, poultry and eggs through a national agricultural policy known as supply management. The system uses production quotas and import controls, including tariffs, to provide farmers with more stable and predictable prices while maintaining domestic supply.

Critics describe the system as protectionist and as a government-backed cartel.

Washington argues that Canada’s supply-management system restricts US dairy exports. Trump posted on Truth Social that “Canada had been ripping off the United States of America for years” and accused it of imposing “ridiculously high tariffs” that made life impossible for US farmers.

Canadian producers reject that argument, saying the existing trade agreement already gives US imports substantial tariff-free access that is not fully utilised.

Canada’s dairy trade deficit with the US has grown significantly since CUSMA came into force on July 1, 2020, according to the Dairy Processors Association of Canada.

In 2020, Canada exported 241.3 million Canadian dollars ($173m) in dairy products to the US and imported 647.4 million Canadian dollars ($462.7m) worth of dairy and dairy products. In 2025, Canadian dairy exports had risen to 308.7 million Canadian dollars ($220.7m) while dairy imports from the US had more than doubled to 1.355 billion Canadian dollars ($968.5m), accounting for 13.8 percent of total value of US dairy exports, according to the association.

Bryan Yu, chief economist at Central 1 credit union, said the immediate shock of losing a major market could be difficult for Canadian producers to absorb because replacement buyers cannot be found quickly.

“There is going to be pain in the near term for a lot of our producers,” Yu told Al Jazeera.

“You really can’t quickly adjust to a 50 percent tariff, because it’s uncharted waters for a lot of industries … and ultimately it shuts [Canadian producers] out, because a lot of them don’t have the margins that they can play with,” he said.

Yu said Canadian consumers might absorb some of the additional supply while exporters search for new markets and higher-value products, but neither adjustment is instantaneous.

“There are global markets as well, especially when you talk about chilled, chilled beef, chilled products and really it’s a question of whether … other types of markets that could be available.”

Canada has also imposed retaliatory tariffs, which came into effect on September 8 and cover $20bn worth of US products.

Dairy products are among the targeted goods. The list includes a 50 percent tariff on milk, cream and whey products and a 25 percent tariff on many cheeses imported from the US.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has framed Ottawa’s response as both retaliation and an attempt to build greater economic resilience.

Announcing the collapse of the latest negotiations, he said Canada would match Washington’s new tariffs “dollar for dollar” to protect workers, farmers, families and businesses.

But retaliatory measures carry risks of their own.

“Canada’s new retaliatory tariffs will help some industries but hurt most and weaken economic growth across the country by raising costs for producers and consumers,” Oxford Economics said in a report.

For now, geography remains important for perishable goods like dairy products that once moved quickly across the US border and cannot be redirected overnight to a distant market without new buyers, logistics and regulatory approvals.

Ottawa’s Trade Commissioner Service is advising affected companies to check their CUSMA compliance, explore available relief and contact trade commissioners about potential new markets.

Yu predicted that the US and Canada could reach a tariff deal in the following months but said the interim period could bring “higher prices, weaker economic activity and deeper mistrust”.

For Pruim, the uncertainty is as destabilising as the tariff threat itself.

“I think, like [for] any Canadian, it’s disappointing to have these trade talks collapse again and just the uncertainty around it.”

articles.title: 9 killed in road accident in Saudi Arabia's Al-Ahsa; 7 from same family
articles.summary: Middle East News: In a devastating collision on the Al-Uqair-Al-Uyun road in Saudi Arabia's Al-Ahsa, 9 people tragically lost their lives, with seven victims belonging to the same family, highlighting the urgent need for road safety measures.
articles.body: Seven members of a family and two others were killed after two vehicles collided on the Al-Uqair-Al-Uyun road in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, Saudi Gazette reported.The crash took place in Al-Ahsa governorate. The seven family members were travelling in one vehicle and included a father, mother, three sons and two daughters. The other vehicle was carrying two young men, both of whom died in the collision.The Eastern Province Traffic Department said its teams responded to the crash and identified a sudden swerve as the cause of the collision. Authorities are completing the necessary procedures.The impact severely damaged both vehicles, leaving people trapped inside the wreckage. Civil Defense and Red Crescent rescue teams were sent to the scene and worked to free those trapped in the vehicles.All nine people died in the crash.The Al-Uqair-Al-Uyun road is an important route in the Eastern Province, connecting parts of Al-Ahsa governorate with the coastal areas.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Hunter charged with fatally shooting a woman he thought was a deer, police say
articles.summary: A 74-year-old man has been charged in the fatal shooting of a woman after he said he mistook her for a deer while hunting, the Delaware State Police said.
articles.body: A 74-year-old man has been charged in the fatal shooting of a woman after he said he mistook her for a deer while hunting, the Delaware State Police said. Walter Moorhead of Salisbury, Maryland, was arrested after troopers responded at about at 7:40 p.m. on Friday to a report of a woman shot in an open field in the town of Ellendale. Troopers provided care before the 39-year-old woman was transported to a hospital, where she was pronounced dead. State police identified the woman Sunday as Santos Maria Chilel Soto of Georgetown, Delaware. Chilel Soto was walking in the field with a man and two children when Moorhead fired at her, according to state police. He was allegedly hunting from a camouflaged shelter, known as a “ground blind,” and believed he saw a deer and fired his rifle, striking Chilel Soto, according to police. Moorhead was charged with manslaughter, reckless endangerment and possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony. He was released on $43,000 cash bond, state police said. Moorhead did not return a phone call requesting comment on Sunday. It was not immediately clear whether he has retained an attorney.

articles.title: Polls close in Russian vote with a near-certain outcome
articles.summary: Polls have closed in Russia’s tightly controlled parliamentary elections with President Vladimir Putin once again set to cement his dominance over domestic politics.
articles.body: Polls have closed in Russia’s tightly controlled parliamentary elections with President Vladimir Putin once again set to cement his dominance over domestic politics. In the absence of credible opposition, the question is not whether but by how much the United Russia party – which backs Putin – will win, although turnout could give an indication of support for the war in Ukraine. In the last parliamentary elections, held in 2021 – before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine – United Russia took 324 of the 450 seats in the Duma, the lower house of the Russian parliament. Putin is not a member of the party, although he served as its leader between 2008 and 2012. As the sitting president, Putin was not on the ballot. He is not up for election until 2030, having won the most recent presidential election in 2024 with just under 88.5% of the vote. Meaningful opposition is effectively nonexistent in Russia, with critics either barred, in jail or exiled abroad. According to the independent human rights monitor OVD-Info, more than 2,000 people are currently in prison for political reasons. Russia’s only registered anti-war party, Yabloko – “Apple” in Russian – was briefly allowed to take part before being barred by the Supreme Court last month from the federal party-lists election. Some individual Yabloko candidates were allowed to run in single-seat local districts, even though the Supreme Court banned the party’s main national list. But these candidates faced significant restrictions and pressures. Two of the party’s deputy leaders were recently imprisoned on charges related to their anti-war stances and social media posts. Yabloko said on Saturday that one of its election observers “lost consciousness” while being detained at a polling station in St. Petersburg. It said numerous other Yabloko observers were barred from polling stations elsewhere. The outcome of the election is likely to be used by the Kremlin to claim a stronger mandate, saying it illustrates Russians’ support for Putin and what the Kremlin calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine. Ahead of the vote, Putin signaled in a televised speech to the nation that the election results will show Russians are united behind the army. “Your choice and determination will show once again that millions of people are backing our fighters and that we stand together, united by shared values, our historical memory, love for our Motherland,” Putin said. Rather than the actual results, observers will likely look at turnout as an indicator of how Russians are feeling about the war and Russia’s political trajectory. Electronic voting questions Polls closed on Sunday after three days of voting across Russia’s 11 time zones and at Russian embassies and consulates abroad. People living in areas of Ukraine that are currently occupied by Russia were also asked to vote, with new constituencies added for Moscow-controlled parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions. Ukraine rejected the elections taking place in its territory, calling them a “farce.” As the elections unfolded, Russia continued to attack its neighbor. According to Kyiv, Moscow fired hundreds of drones and several missiles against Ukrainian cities over the election period. Separately, Kyiv launched one of its largest attacks against Moscow overnight into Sunday. More than 1,500 drones were launched, killing at least two people and damaging a major oil refinery. After debuting the option during the last election in 2021, online and electronic voting was widely available – and encouraged – this time around. Moscow went as far as offering its residents incentives in the form of points for prizes, if they chose to vote electronically instead of casting a paper ballot. Some voters in Moscow told the independent Russian news outlet SotaVision they weren’t issued paper ballots because of “malfunctions” and were encouraged to vote via an electronic terminal instead. “They did this on purpose, the b****rds,” one voter told SotaVision. Critics have long been suspicious of the Kremlin’s introduction of electronic voting because they argue it’s less transparent. Russian authorities reject criticism of their electoral processes and insist elections are held in accordance with the law. Putin himself opted to vote online, with the Kremlin releasing a video showing him navigating the online system and casting his vote. Russian state news agency TASS reported outages and malfunctions of the electronic voting system in Moscow on Friday into Saturday, quoting Central Election Commission chair Ella Pamfilova as saying this was due to a “very large-scale and intense” attack.

articles.title: Daughter of Julianne Jaillet hopes advances in DNA testing will help solve her mother’s cold case
articles.summary: Julianne Jaillet disappeared from Bellevue, Washington, in June 1985. Light the Way is supporting her daughter, who hopes DNA will help solve the cold case.
articles.body: In June 1985, 36-year-old Julianne Jaillet disappeared, leaving behind 10-year-old daughter, Tammy McAdams. More than four decades later, Tammy is still hoping to learn what happened to her mother. Tammy and her mom were close. Julianne was a single mom and Tammy was her only child. Tammy says they loved spending time together, shopping, doing “all the fun things you do with your mom.” They lived in Washington and moved a couple of times during Tammy’s childhood, including from Ballard to Lynnwood to live with Julianne’s boyfriend, Ian Jaillet. Tammy says she remembers living there for about a year. “I guess things got bad between them, and then they split up, and he pretty much left us stranded,” Tammy told Dateline. “My grandparents went and got us.” Tammy says Julianne and Ian had an on-and-off relationship. In 1985, Julianne was back together with Ian, and the two quietly got married that January. Tammy stayed with her grandparents because she was in school and her mom worked nights in a nursing home. “My grandparents said, ‘OK, we’re gonna keep her till the end of the school year and let you work nights because, you know, you don’t have someone to watch her when it’s just you and her,’” Tammy told Dateline. Tammy did not see her mom every day during the school year. Her mom’s house was about 30 minutes away from her grandparents’ place. Tammy last saw her mom on May 25. “My last memory was really good,” she shared. They went shopping at Bellevue Square and had lunch together. Tammy says she remembers going back to her mom’s house in Bellevue for a bit, where she lived with Ian. “I did not care for him, so I did not want to stay the night,” Tammy said. She was driven back to her grandparents’ house. In June, Julianne’s family learned she was missing. Tammy’s grandparents sat her down to share the news. “It was just confusing,” Tammy said. “I was a young girl.” Tammy was sent to Minnesota to live with her aunt and uncle for the summer, while her grandparents dug into Julianne’s disappearance. “I think my family just kept me sort of distracted and busy,” Tammy explained. “I don’t think I was old enough to really comprehend what was happening.” Tammy’s aunt Margaret was the last family member known to have spoken with Julianne. The two talked on the phone after Margaret received a letter from Julianne in the mail. “She said my mom was happy. She was in a new home with Ian,” Tammy said. “She was buying new furniture.” Tammy now has that letter. According to Tammy, who says she has read her mom’s case file, Ian told authorities that he and Julianne got into an argument, and she took off. “June 1st is the date he claims they had the heated argument,” Tammy said. “My aunt said she spoke with her a few days before that.” Tammy says her mom did not drive, and doesn’t know where Julianne would have gone on her own. She also says that her grandparents convinced Ian to call the police and report Julianne missing. Ian reported Julianne missing to the Bellevue Police Department on June 18, more than two weeks after he said they had argued and Julianne left. Dateline contacted the Bellevue Police Department for an interview regarding Julianne’s case. The interview request was declined. Bellevue PD provided Dateline with the initial missing persons report and supplemental reports in Julianne’s case file. According to the missing persons report, Ian stated that he and Julianne got into a fight and she left on June 1, around 1:30 a.m., telling him “that she was never coming back.” He stated that Julianne had left before, “but never this long.” The report states that Julianne left on foot, and that one suitcase and her clothes were gone. However, when a Bellevue PD detective spoke to Ian on the phone on June 20, Ian told the detective “he left the house and upon his return [Julianne] had left,” the detective wrote in the police report. “I asked the reason for the delay in making the report. He stated he had kept thinking she would return.” Dateline reached out to Ian Jaillet about Julianne’s disappearance and has not yet received a response. According to the police report, in 1986, Ian was asked if he was responsible for his wife’s disappearance. He denied any responsibility. The report states that in April of that year, Ian “submitted to a polygraph examination” and the “result of the test was inconclusive.” The report states that Bellevue PD detectives met with Ian in 2009 and again asked him if he had any involvement in his wife’s disappearance. “I asked Ian if he had murdered Julianne and he said that he did not. I asked him if he had any knowledge whatsoever as to where Julianne was and he said that he did not,” the detective assigned to the case at the time wrote in the report. Two weeks after Julianne vanished, her purse containing some personal items was found at the MGM Grand Hotel in Reno, Nevada. According to the police report, “the items were found on 06-14-85 by an unknown guest on the 22nd floor. The items were sitting on a couch in the hallway.” Bellevue PD spoke on the phone with the hotel’s head of security. The report continues, “In checking his records in June from the 12th to the 17th, he has no record of the missing person being registered at the hotel.” According to the police report, the purse and its contents were shipped back to Washington on June 18. Tammy says most of the purse’s contents were typical: an ID card, glasses, lipstick. “Nothing that would make me think she went out of town,” she said. “But there was a pair of underwear,” Tammy told Dateline. “I mean, that’s just not -- not normal.” According to the police report, the purse and its contents were obtained from Ian in July 1985 and placed into evidence. In 2002, a Bellevue PD detective sent items from the purse to the Washington State Patrol Crime Lab for DNA extraction. DNA was later taken from Tammy, her grandmother, and Ian. The crime lab used Tammy’s DNA to confirm that the items in the purse belonged to Julianne. Julianne’s DNA profile was subsequently uploaded to CODIS. Tammy is hopeful that DNA will help untangle her mother’s case. “I’m so thankful for technology,” Tammy said. “The advancement in DNA is amazing.” Over the years, Bellevue PD has compared Julianne’s DNA to multiple Jane Does in the area. No matches have been made, according to the police report. As the decades passed, Tammy took up her family’s push for answers. When she was in college, Tammy became the one asking the questions. “I’ve been working on it for, like, 30 years myself,” she said. Tammy’s grandmother died in 2020, without knowing what happened to her daughter. Tammy says one of the last conversations she had with her grandmother was about how much she missed Julianne. Tammy’s aunt Margaret has also died. In 2023, Tammy started sharing her mom’s story on TikTok to gather support and increase attention. “I would say, at first, it was a little tough for me. I think I can be private at times,” she shared. But she says posting has helped her come out of her shell and has connected her with others in similar situations. “Social media, I think, offers a lot of family,” she said. “People will contact you and give you even more, you know, ideas, suggestions.” Another resource for Tammy has been Light the Way, a volunteer-led organization that supports families whose loved one is missing or whose homicide is unresolved. Shayna Richard founded the Light the Way Missing Persons Advocacy Project in 2020. Light the Way has featured dozens of cases, including Julianne’s. “A big part of what we do, especially in those older, unresolved, long-term missing cases like Julianne, is we provide awareness opportunities. Whether that’s billboards, flyers, introductions to podcasters,” Shayna told Dateline. Shayna says she was an avid true crime consumer before creating Light the Way and was drawn to advocacy through the missing persons cases of Gabby Petito and Oakley Carlson. Shayna says those cases introduced her to the large online presence of families with missing loved ones. “Gabby’s story kind of brought me to that community of people,” she said. “And through Oakley’s story, I learned how to be an advocate.” Light the Way meets families where they are in the process. “It’s not an easy road at all for families to navigate. There’s no booklet,” Shayna said. “You can always reach out to us.” Tammy’s years of digging have led her to develop theories about what happened to Julianne, but no definitive answers. She says she’ll keep working on her mother’s case until it’s solved. She has no plans to give up. “I see it as a cold case; I just don’t have the closure of her remains,” she said. “They might not ever be found, but I still have hope.” She also holds on to the memory of her mother’s smile and her love of life. At the time of her disappearance, Julianne was 5’7” and 125 lbs., with reddish-brown hair and green eyes. She would be 77 years old today. If you have information about Julianne’s case, please call the Bellevue Police Department at 425-452-6917 or the non-emergency line at 425-577-5656. You can email the department at bellevuepd@bellevuewa.gov. If you have a story to share with Dateline, please submit it here.

articles.title: India A vs Australia A multi-format series: Full list of squads and schedule as Devdutt Padikkal and Ruturaj Gaikwad named captains
articles.summary: With Devdutt Padikkal set for India's A series against Australia, here's a look at the full Indian squad and the schedule.
articles.body:
Devdutt Padikkal will captain India A's multi-day side against Australia A.

Ruturaj Gaikwad will lead the one-day squad, with Hardik Pandya included subject to fitness.

Devdutt Padikkal to lead India A in the multi-day matches.

All five matches will be played in Puducherry from September 22 to October 11.

India A ready for their games vs Australia A

India A's squads for the home series against Australia A carry genuine selection weight this time around, given the tour doubles as a final trial run for several Test hopefuls ahead of next year's Border-Gavaskar Trophy.

The BCCI announced the squads on Wednesday, with two different captains handed charge across the multi-day and one-day legs.

Devdutt Padikkal leads the four-day squad, with Sai Sudharsan as his deputy, fresh off a series in which both were central to India's Test win over Sri Lanka. Ruturaj Gaikwad takes charge of the one-day side, with Padikkal doubling up as his vice-captain across formats.

The inclusion of Hardik Pandya in the one-day squad, subject to fitness clearance, is the most eye-catching name on the list, offering the all-rounder a route back into competitive cricket after his prolonged injury lay-off. Australia A are yet to announce their own squad for the series.

The presence of former IPL player Laxmipathy Balaji as the head coach is also guaranteed to boost their chances against the Aussies.

articles.title: 'Could change a lot': Zelenskky and Trump to meet in New York ahead of UNGA
articles.summary: US News: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday said that he spoke with US President Donald Trump and that the two agreed to meet in New York, addin.
articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday said that he spoke with US President Donald Trump and that the two agreed to meet in New York, adding that the meeting “could change a lot” as diplomatic momentum builds around efforts to end the war in Ukraine. Trump will be coming to New York for the United Nations General Assembly.“I just spoke with President Trump. An important conversation, and we got through a lot. We agreed to meet in New York, and this meeting could change a lot. There is diplomatic momentum,” Zelenskyy said in a post on X.Zelenskyy said he thanked Trump for the visit to Kyiv by US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. “We went through the key details thoroughly, and they saw the situation in Ukraine firsthand,” he said.“The peace track is our number one priority,” Zelenskyy said, adding that there were ideas for de-escalation steps and for addressing fundamental security issues, including energy security, food security and the protection of human life.“We are working together with the American team and are ready to take really serious steps,” he said.Zelenskyy also thanked Trump for signing the Lindsey Graham bill into law, saying “We all concur – there must be peace." “Thank you to everyone who stands with Ukraine!
